teaser: Seven releases in one afternoon turned the reading meter into a working model: pay after you read, and the rating sets the price.
core_idea: On 10 October the reading meter became a working pay-on-demand publication in seven releases in 3 hours 40 minutes: pay for the share read from a balance that can go below zero, rate usefulness after reading to set the price from free to double, personas and newsrooms kept in the reader's browser, and consented, encrypted sharing for a designed front page. Paying after the value inverts Leanpub's pay-before model and is supported, with caveats, by pay-what-you-want evidence; Blendle's refunds show ratings measure quality. Each feature grew from using the last, which a Wardley map shows: new components on the left, built on commodities already there. It was fast because of non-functional work done before. Every decision started from not ripping off the reader. What is missing is traffic.

quotes.text: The only question left is whether people will pay for it.
If you saw the value, pay; if you saw more value, pay more; if you did not, do not.

quotes.text: The afternoon was cheap because the right-hand side of the map was already built.

figures.caption: The reading meter at the end of 10 October, as a Wardley map: everything added that afternoon sits on the left, built on components that already existed on the right. The animated version, one release at a time, is in How it grew.
The reader card at the foot of an article: what it cost, how much was read, the reading list, and the three ratings. Usefulness sets the price; the other two shape the newsroom.
Your newsroom: a front page for one persona at a time, built in your browser from what you read.
The reading account: the balance, what was spent, and the controls. Kept in this browser, and only here.
Send us your reading: exactly what would be sent, word for word, then copy it or send it encrypted with your consent.
Every decision this afternoon was a choice between charging more now and making the reader glad they paid.
The afternoon from git: seven steps of the reading meter in 3 hours 40 minutes, and seven other pieces of work released in the same four hours.
The afternoon as a Wardley map, one release at a time: what already existed, then each feature as it was added and what it was built on, ending with what comes next. Times are UTC, from the commits.
The same story at a larger scale, built up one layer at a time: each layer matured until it was invisible, and that is what made the next one possible.
The whole zigzag. Solid arrows are a thing maturing, until it is invisible; dashed arrows are what its maturity made possible, one layer up.
